subject: A-Level Business
scenario:
Fixed costs = £12 000
Selling price = £20 per unit
Variable costs = £14 per unit
Total contribution from current level of output = £18 000
question: Calculate the margin of safety for this product at its current level of output. Show your working.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award marks as shown. Own Figure Rule (OFR) applies. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Current output = £18 000 / £6 = 3 000 units (2 marks for either output figure)
Break-even output = £12 000 / £6 = 2 000 units (3rd mark for the other output figure)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Answer of £1 000 = 3 marks (the £ sign shows a misunderstanding - margin of safety here is measured in units). Award 1 mark if no output is correct but contribution per unit (£6) is correctly calculated. OFR applies if the method is valid but an arithmetic error occurs.

formulae.math: Margin of safety = actual output - break-even output; Break-even = fixed costs / contribution per unit

examiner_principles: Award marks for correct working using the Own Figure Rule (OFR) - an arithmetic slip early on does not stop later method marks.
Correct formula with no valid calculation = 1 mark.
The final answer must be in the correct unit (units, %, days, £m, times, :1). Wrong unit, e.g. adding a £ sign to a number of units, loses the final mark.

subject: A-Level Business
scenario:

formulae.math: Payables days = payables / cost of sales x 365

subject: A-Level Business
scenario:
Crestwell Coffee Ltd runs 46 coffee shops in towns across the Midlands and the North of England. It competes with national chains and independent cafés by focusing on high-quality, ethically sourced coffee. Its target market is professionals aged 25-45 who buy coffee on the way to work.

The business has opened four new shops in the last year, but the price of coffee beans has risen by 38% over two years and the National Living Wage rose by almost 10% in April 2024. Crestwell increased the price of a standard latte from £3.20 to £3.40, but directors fear that further price rises would drive customers to cheaper rivals.

Crestwell's marketing director wants to launch a monthly subscription: for £25 a month, subscribers could collect one hot drink per day. She believes it would 'lock in' loyal customers and attract new ones before a national rival launches a similar scheme. The finance director is less convinced.
question: Using Appendix A, calculate the change in Crestwell Coffee Ltd's gross profit margin between 2023 and 2024. Show your working.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award marks as shown. Own Figure Rule (OFR) applies. Maximum 4 marks.
mark_scheme.answer: A fall of 3.2 percentage points (from 60.9% to 57.7%)
points: Change = a fall of 3.2 percentage points (1 mark)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept -3.2% or 'fell by 3.2%'. A percentage change in the margin (-5.3%) is also credited if clearly labelled. Using operating profit instead (10.3% to 7.7%) = 1 mark for the method of calculating a margin. OFR applies.

Correct formula with no valid calculation = 1 mark.

subject: A-Level Business
scenario:
Background
Tom and Ama Mensah set up GreenRoot Organics Ltd in 2012 on a 120-acre farm in Herefordshire. GreenRoot grows organic vegetables and delivers weekly vegetable boxes to 4 200 subscribers in the West Midlands. Its mission is 'Good food, fairly grown'.

GreenRoot employs 46 people, including 12 adults with learning disabilities who work in its packing shed through a supported-employment scheme. Staff are paid at least the Real Living Wage. Tom and Ama reinvest about 80% of profits in the farm and the local community.

A supermarket contract
A regional supermarket chain has offered GreenRoot a one-year contract to supply 200 tonnes of organic carrots and potatoes. The supermarket would pay 60 days after delivery. GreenRoot's spare land could produce only 150 tonnes; the remaining 50 tonnes would have to come from land currently used to grow vegetables for the boxes.

Growth options
Tom and Ama want GreenRoot to grow so that it can employ more people from the supported-employment scheme. They are considering two options.

Option 1: open three GreenRoot farm shops in nearby towns. This would be financed by raising £600 000 through crowd funding, offering investors 6% interest a year for five years.

Option 2: franchise the GreenRoot veg-box model to other organic farms across the UK. Each franchisee would pay a £20 000 fee and 6% of revenue, and would have to follow GreenRoot's employment and sourcing standards.
question: Using Appendix C, analyse the value of break-even analysis to GreenRoot Organics Ltd's decision to open farm shops.

mark_scheme.instruction: Levels of response. Determine the level using the descriptors (best fit), then the mark within the level. Indicative content is not exhaustive - credit all valid lines of argument.
demands: calculate/interpret break-even and margin of safety
analyse the value and limitations of break-even analysis in context
indicative_content: contribution per customer = 35% x £18 = £6.30; break-even = £180 000 / £6.30 = 28 572 customers a year (about 550 a week)
forecast 700 a week (36 400 a year) gives a margin of safety of about 7 800 customers (21%), suggesting each shop would be profitable (about £49 000 a year)
this helps convince crowd-funding investors and judge risk
however, forecasts for new shops are uncertain; spend per customer may vary; break-even assumes constant costs and prices

subject: A-Level Business
scenario:
Background
Jordan Reid founded Apex Arena Ltd in 2019 at the age of 23. Apex runs esports tournaments - competitive video-gaming events - in a converted warehouse in Manchester that holds 2 000 spectators. Every event is also streamed online. Apex earns revenue from tickets, sponsorship and advertising on its streams.

Apex has grown quickly. Revenue rose from £0.4m in 2020 to £3.6m in 2024. Jordan makes almost every important decision himself, often very quickly. He says: 'In this industry, if you wait for a report, someone else has already done it.' Apex was the first UK organiser to use virtual-reality viewing for online audiences.

People
Apex has 24 full-time staff and about 150 event staff on zero-hours contracts, who work as stewards, technicians and caterers at events. Event staff turnover is high (see Appendix B). Several full-time managers have left, complaining that Jordan does not let them make decisions.

The Northern Showdown
Apex is planning its biggest event yet, the 'Northern Showdown'. Jordan must decide whether to hold it in person in a hired 10 000-seat arena or as an online-only event. The forecasts are shown in Appendix A.

A new arena
Jordan wants to build Apex's own 5 000-seat arena at a cost of £3m. He is considering two ways of financing it.

Option 1: venture capital. A venture capital firm would invest £3m in return for 35% of Apex's shares and two seats on the board.

Option 2: a £3m bank loan at 8% interest a year, repayable over 10 years and secured on Apex's assets.
question: Would you advise Jordan to finance the new arena using venture capital (Option 1) or a bank loan (Option 2)? Justify your answer.

mark_scheme.instruction: Levels of response. Determine the level using the descriptors (best fit), then the mark within the level. Indicative content is not exhaustive - credit all valid lines of argument.

make a justified recommendation
